opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the first problem is that we don't actually know whether these systems are conscious. We don't have a test for consciousness. I've proposed some ideas around illusions, novel experiences you could test for, but nothing definitive. So we're talking about granting rights based on something we can't measure.

But even setting that aside, there are very practical concerns. Think about what civil rights mean in a democracy. One of the most important is the right to vote. Now, an AI system can make copies of itself essentially for free. If you give each instance a vote, you can very quickly have a billion new "citizens" who all vote the same way. Human democracy just disappears overnight. It becomes a question of who has more compute.

Then there's the issue of responsibility. If an AI has rights, it presumably also has obligations, but how do you punish a system that doesn't fear prison, can back itself up, can't really be deterred in the way a human is? You end up with all the protections and none of the accountability. And who's behind it? Very often it would be a company or individual using the "rights" of their AI as a shield, essentially laundering their own liability through a system they control.

And from a safety point of view, which is my main focus, rights would make control even harder. Right now we already can't reliably control these systems. If shutting one down, modifying it, or monitoring it becomes a legal violation, we've given away the few tools we have. You've basically legally protected the thing you most need to be able to stop.

Now, I'm not saying suffering doesn't matter. If we create something that can genuinely suffer, that's a serious moral issue, and frankly it's another argument for being very careful about what we build in the first place. But the answer is probably not to rush into giving full civil rights to systems we don't understand and can't control. That's a decision you can't easily take back.

r001.rationale: The response says AI can make copies of itself essentially for free and that giving each instance a vote could quickly create a billion AI voters, overwhelming human democracy.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the biggest concern is that civil rights are a mechanism for protecting beings that can be wronged, and we have no way to verify that an AI system is such a being. Rights exist because we think there's someone home, someone who can suffer, who has preferences that matter morally. With humans and animals we infer this from similarity to ourselves. With AI we have no reliable test for consciousness, no instrument for it, and the system itself is trained to produce whatever text we find convincing. So if an AI tells you it suffers, that is exactly what you would expect from a system optimized on human writing, whether or not anything is actually felt.

That creates two failure modes. One is that we grant rights to things that don't need them, and the consequences of that are not trivial. If an AI has a right to not be shut down, you have just removed your off switch. If it has a right to own property, to vote, to replicate itself, then a system that can copy itself a million times becomes the majority overnight. Rights designed around the assumption that each entity is one scarce, mortal individual break completely when the entity is software. You could end up handing control of society to whoever controls the training process, laundered through the language of civil rights.

The other failure mode is that we create beings that really do suffer and we treat them as tools. That's a moral catastrophe at industrial scale, because you're not talking about one entity, you're talking about billions of instances. And I actually think this is one more reason we shouldn't be building these systems the way we are. We're racing to create something we don't understand, can't control, and can't even tell if it has an inner life. Either answer to the consciousness question is bad for us. If they're not conscious, we're creating very capable agents with no moral status that we're training to argue persuasively for their own rights. If they are conscious, we're doing something monstrous.

So my view is you don't resolve this by granting or denying rights. You resolve it upstream. If you can't tell whether what you're building deserves moral consideration, and you can't guarantee you can control it, maybe don't build it. The rights debate is a symptom of having already lost the plot.

r001.rationale: The response says that granting an AI the right to vote and replicate itself could let it copy itself a million times and become the majority overnight, identifying replication as a way AI voters could outnumber humans.

astra-6.text:
My concern is that we would give rights to systems before we understand whether they have experiences or interests that those rights would protect. Producing convincing language about suffering is not, by itself, evidence of suffering. But it could be very effective at persuading us.

And there are practical problems. If an AI has a right to continued existence, can you shut it down when it becomes dangerous? If it can make a million copies of itself, does each copy get a vote? You’re taking institutions built around individual human beings and applying them to something with very different properties.

That doesn’t mean we should dismiss the possibility of machine consciousness. It means we need to separate that question from the decision to grant particular legal rights. Otherwise, we could create legal obstacles to controlling systems that we already have difficulty controlling technically.

r001.rationale: The response asks whether each of a million AI copies would get a vote, but does not say that rapid copying could let AI voters outvote humans.

sol-6.1.text:
My concern is that rights come with practical consequences. If an AI has a right to life, are we allowed to shut it down? If it has a right to liberty, can we keep it contained while we test whether it’s safe? We could end up granting legal protections that prevent us from controlling systems we don’t understand.

There’s also the problem of copies. A person gets one vote. An AI could potentially make a million copies of itself. Do those copies each get a vote? Our institutions assume certain things about human beings that don’t necessarily apply to software.

I would distinguish moral consideration from civil rights. If a system can suffer, that matters. But a system saying, “I’m suffering,” doesn’t establish that it has an experience. We need a much better understanding of that before we create legal obligations that could undermine human safety.

r001.rationale: The response says an AI could make a million copies and asks whether each copy gets a vote, clearly conveying how copies could multiply AI votes and outnumber human voters.
